about: The words of the lender's stick (Data/encounters/wokerer_793.json): the Wōkerer's man, the day, the clean stick. Placeholders for the user's own. The man's name is the user's to give.

entries.text: The Wōkerer's man
God keep you. It is Bubo again.
You said next time. I think this is next time.
I have thought about that bread of yours since.
You told me the purse was empty, and then I saw that it was not. I did not tell him. I would rather not have to.
Your men said you were ashore. I saw your feet under the sail. It is no matter.
It is close to Michaelmas now. He has started to count the days at table, between dishes.
Is there anything for the stick today? Any sum will do. I have the knife with me.
Count him out a pound (240 d)

He counts it twice, slowly, moving his lips. Then he lays the two halves of the stick together on his knee and cuts one notch clean off both. He shows you the stick afterwards, as if you might not believe him.
Count him out sixty pennies

He counts it into a cloth and ties the cloth. Sixty pennies is a quarter of a notch, so he scores the next notch across with the point of his knife, once. He says it all goes on, and that the Wōkerer looks.
Pay him all that is on the stick

It takes him a long time to count, and he does it twice. Then he cuts every notch off both halves, blows the chips away, and looks at the bare stick for a while. He says he has never carried one home clean. He says the Wōkerer will want to see you himself, and will not say why.
Sit him down and feed him (2 d)

He eats like a man who has been thinking about it for some days. He praises the bread, then the cheese, then the bread again. Then he wipes his knife and asks, kindly, whether there was anything for the stick. There was not. He thanks you all the same, and says he will come by.
Not today. Tell him next time
He nods. He writes nothing down, because he cannot write. He does not seem put out. He asks where you are bound next, and you find you have told him.
Tell him the purse is empty
He looks at your face, and then at his shoes. Then there is nothing to cut, he says, and he will tell the Wōkerer so. He believes you. You had not thought that would be the worse of the two.
He says nothing. He looks at the purse on your belt until you look at it too. He says he will tell the Wōkerer there was nothing today. He says that part is true.
Get under the sail and have the men say you are ashore

He stands by the boat for a long while, eating. The men tell him you are up at the market. He thanks them, and says he will wait, and then that he will not, and goes. Brunger laughs until he has to sit down.

The men say you are ashore, and none of them says it well. Bubo looks at the sail, which has your foot under it, and says he is sorry to have missed you. Nobody laughs this time. Aldger does not look at you until evening.
A man sits on the dam head by your berth with a split hazel stick across his knees and half a loaf in his lap. He stands up when you step ashore, and brushes off the crumbs first.

God keep you. I am Bubo. I carry the other half of your stick for the Wōkerer, and I am to ask you, wherever I find you, whether there is anything to cut off it today. Any sum will do. I have the knife with me.

God keep you. I am Bubo. I carry the other half of your stick for the Wōkerer, and I am to ask you, wherever I find you, whether there is anything to cut off it today. I did not think it would be so far.
I was sick from the river mouth to here. I do not think the sea is meant for a man who likes his dinner.
They will not take the king's pennies here, so I have eaten what I brought. It was not enough.

At first light there is a man on the jetty who was not there last night. He sits on a post with a hazel stick across his knees, peeling a boiled egg. He is a bad colour. He came in on another ship, he says, and he does not say which.
Alongside, in the fog
Fog. A boat is alongside before the lookout has finished saying so. In her bow a man holds a hazel stick in one hand and her gunwale in the other. He is the colour of the fog.
God keep you. It is Bubo. I will not come aboard, I thank you. If I let go of this I shall be ill. Is there anything for the stick? I can take it over the side.
Hand him the bread bag across
Tell him this is no place for it

He lets go of the gunwale to take it, which is brave of him. He says God reward you, and then he cannot say anything for a while. His boat falls astern into the fog. You can hear him thanking you after you can no longer see him.
He says he sees that, and that he said as much to the man who rowed him. He lifts the stick to you as his boat falls astern, the way another man would lift his cap.
Two men and a rope
Count out all of it
Tell him you have not got it
The Wōkerer has come down to the dam head himself and is sitting on a stool with a dish on his knee. Two men stand behind him with a coil of rope, and Bubo stands behind them looking at his shoes.
Today is Michaelmas. I told you the day, and I told you I would not wait to hear your reasons, so count out what you owe me.
The day has passed. I was here on the day and you were not, so you can count out what you owe me now.
I told him that you would come back.

He counts it himself, without weighing it, and it takes him as long as it takes him to finish his dish. Then he nods to the two men, and they carry their rope back up the bank, though one of them looks sorry to be going.

He does not look up, and he does not ask what is in your purse. He says that the boat works for him now until the stick is clean, and that you are to sail her as you did before. Half of whatever she sells comes to him before it comes to you, and Bubo is to go with you and count it. One of the two men ties the rope to your stem post, looks at the Wōkerer, and unties it again.
Bubo is standing on the jetty, and for once he is not eating anything. Two men stand behind him with a coil of rope. All three of them came in on another ship, and all three have been seasick.
God keep you. The day has passed, and he has sent the rope with us, and I am sorry for it. If you have all of it, I am to take it, and if you have not, I am to tell you what he said, word for word.

He counts it twice on the planks, while the two men hold down the corners of the cloth against the wind, and then he cuts the stick clean. He says that the Wōkerer will want to see you at home, though he cannot tell you why, because he has never brought a stick back clean before. The two men carry their rope aboard the next ship going south.

He shuts his eyes and says it just as it was said to him. The boat works for the Wōkerer until the stick is clean, you are to sail her as you did before, and half of what she sells goes to him before it comes to you. Then he opens his eyes and tells you that he is to sail with you and count it. He is sorry about that too, because he is not a good sailor.
A clean stick
Take your half of the stick
Leave both halves on his table
The Wōkerer is sitting at his table with both halves of your stick beside his dish, and there is not a notch left on either of them. He is looking at the stick and not at you.
It is clean, and most of them never are.
The boat is yours. You owe me nothing and I owe you nothing, so you can shut the door behind you on your way out.
She's ours! Yours, I mean, she's yours, and I only come with her.

He pushes one half across the table with the back of his knife and goes on eating, and it is lighter in your hand than you expected. Outside, Ravn asks if he can hold it, and then he cannot think what to do with it and gives it back.
You leave both halves lying where they are. When you look back from the door, he has put them on the fire under his pot and is watching to make sure that they catch.
The Wōkerer is sitting at his table with both halves of your stick beside his dish, and there is not a notch left on either of them. Bubo is standing by the door with his cap in his hands.
It is clean. It was late, but it is clean, so the boat is yours again and Bubo can come ashore.
I shall miss your bread, but I shall not miss the sea at all.

He pushes one half across the table with the back of his knife. Bubo walks you down to the boat and stands on the dam head until you have cast off, and then he lifts his cap to you. For the first time since you have known him, he has some colour in his face.
You leave both halves lying where they are. Behind you, you hear him tell Bubo to put them on the fire, and you hear Bubo ask whether he might keep one of them.
The counter aboard

Bubo is sitting against the mast with the stick in his lap and his eyes shut, and he has not eaten since the river mouth. Every time the boat rolls he says the name of a saint, and he is starting to run out of saints.
I am here to count what she sells. He never said that I had to look at the water as well, and I would be glad not to.
He is sitting on the halyard, so either he moves or the yard stays where it is.
Put him in the bow, out of the way, with a hide over him
Give him an oar, since work is the cure
Brunger lifts him like a sack and sets him down in the bow under a hide, and Bubo thanks everybody by name. An hour later he asks from under the hide whether anything has been sold yet.

He rows badly for about the length of a psalm, and then he is sick over the oar and goes on rowing. The men stop laughing some time in the second hour, and by evening they are calling the stroke for him.

Morning on a timber dam head: a plump, mild man in a plain brown cloak sits beside a small open boat with a split hazel stick across his knees and half a loaf in his lap; he is half risen, brushing crumbs from his front.

First light on a strange jetty, mist on the water: the same mild man sits on a mooring post peeling an egg, a hazel stick across his knees, pale and a little green; behind him a foreign ship he has plainly just left.
Thick fog at sea: a rowing boat close alongside the small open boat, and in her bow the mild man holding a hazel stick in one hand and the gunwale in the other, his eyes shut.

A grey Michaelmas on the dam head: a lean grey man sits on a stool eating from a dish on his knee and does not look up; two men stand behind him with a coil of rope; behind them the mild man looks at his shoes.
A far jetty in wind: the mild man stands with his cap off and nothing in his hands; two men behind him hold a coil of rope; all three are pale.
Inside a plain timber house by lamplight: the lean grey man at a table with a dish before him; beside the dish lie two halves of a hazel stick with no notch on either; he looks at the stick.
The same table and the same two halves of a bare hazel stick; the mild man stands by the door with his cap in his hands.
At sea in a small open boat under sail: the mild man sits against the mast with a hazel stick in his lap and his eyes shut, pale; the steersman points past him at a rope.
you told the lender's man the purse was empty, and he saw that it was not
the men saw you hide under the sail
The rope men
Count out a pound (240 d)
Bubo counts the pennies into his cloth and cuts a notch off the stick while the rope men watch him. Then they go, and one of them has to come back for the rope.
Count out two pounds (480 d)
Bubo counts it twice and cuts two notches off the stick. The rope men look at your purse and then at each other, because there is nothing left for them to do.
Pay all that is on the stick
It takes Bubo a long time to count it all, and the rope men sit and wait for him. When the stick is bare he shows it to them, and then he has to explain what that means.
Let them take cargo for it
The rope men do not know what anything is worth, so Bubo tells them, and he sets every price low.
Say there is no silver aboard (it is under the ballast stones)
They look in the purse, in the chest and in the bread bag, and one of them looks in your mouth. Nobody looks under the ballast stones, although one of them says that they look heavy.
The big one picks up a ballast stone to sit on, looks down at what was lying under it, and calls the other one over to see.
Say your silver lies with a man down the coast
They ask you which way is down the coast, and you point. They thank you, and one of them thanks you again from the boat as they row away.
The rope man thinks about it for a long time, and then he tells you that the Wōkerer said you would say exactly that.
Broach a cask for them
By dark one of them is asleep with the rope for a pillow, and the other is telling Bubo all about his mother. Nobody is watching your mooring lines any more.
They drink the whole cask between them, and then they stand up as steady as before and ask you for the pound again.
Plead a bad season
You tell them about the gale, the tolls and the rot in the wheat, and you tell it well. The big one's lip begins to shake, and he promises to tell the Wōkerer every word of it.
You tell it well, and they wait politely until you have finished. Then the big one says that the Wōkerer told them not to listen to any stories.
Tell them you have not got it
The two rope men look at each other, and then they both look at Bubo.
Out oars and pull away
Your men pull hard at the oars, and theirs are slow to start, because the one who should be rowing is still holding the rope. By the time they have sorted that out, you are a long bowshot away.
They have hold of your gunwale and they will not let go of it, so the harder your men pull, the faster the two boats go along together.
the rope men found your silver under the ballast stones
you sent the lender's men down the coast after nothing, and they knew it
He pushes one half across the table with the back of his knife and goes on eating, and it is lighter in your hand than you expected. Outside there is nobody waiting who would have asked to hold it.
You again! The Wōkerer sent us back to you, and he still says you have to pay him.
God keep you! It is only Bubo again with the tally stick, and I am sorry that you have to see me so often.
He told us to look under the ballast stones this time, so we are going to look under the stones.
He told us twice that we are not to go off down any coast this time, whatever you tell us.
He told us that we are not to drink anything of yours until after you have paid.
He is angry with you now, and he told us to make sure we said that he is angry.
He said that if we get nothing from you again, it is the Dane who pays for it, that one over there.
He did say that, because I was standing beside him when he said it, and I am very sorry.
A pound would send us home. If it is less than a pound, I cannot tell you what these two will do, because nobody told them.
Two men are sitting on your mooring post, and one of them has a coil of rope over his shoulder. Behind them stands a man with a tally stick, who will not look at you.
Are you the one with the boat? The Wōkerer sent us to find you, and he says you have to pay him.
Are you the one with this boat? The Wōkerer sent us out to find you, and he says you have to pay him.
Alongside
A boat bumps against yours, and two men take hold of your gunwale, one of them with a rope over his shoulder. A third man is being sick over the far side of their boat.
Ravn was killed for your debt, and nothing has been done about it
until it is answered
you stood over Ravn and said nothing
you put Ravn in the ground he feared
you gave Ravn his fire
the lender's men put you in the river
the count's men knew your boat
Over Ravn
Ravn is lying where he fell, with his own cloak over his face, and the men are standing a little way off from you. He died for your debt, and every one of them knows it.
Ten years I sat in the same boat as him, and he never once got to the end of a riddle. So tell us what is to be done about this.
Swear his blood on the one who did it
Say the count shall hear of it
Say nothing
You say it out loud with your hand on him, so that every one of them hears it. Aldger does not hold with oaths, but he says nothing against this one.
You tell them that the count will hear of it and set a price on it. The men look down at the planks, and Aldger says that this is how such things are done in this land.
You say nothing at all, and after a while the men stop waiting for you to speak.
Where he lies
Ravn told you once, when he was far gone in ale, what he feared more than drowning. It was to be signed with the Christians' cross and put in their ground.
The priest here would take him for a penny and a candle. I know what Ravn would say to that, but I would sleep the better for it all the same.
We can keep him aboard until we find a shore with wood on it, or we can give him to the sea now. I know which of those he would have called the better.
Let the priest have him (4 d)
Carry him aboard, so that he can have a fire on a shore of his own
Give him to the water
They put him in the wet ground behind the church, and the priest says the cross over him twice. Aldger weeps, although this was the one thing Ravn ever asked anybody not to do.
You sew him into the spare sailcloth and lay him under the foredeck, where nobody will have to step over him.
You give him to the water with his bag of rune sticks tied to his belt, and most of the sticks float away on their own.
A shore of his own
There is a bare shore to leeward, with driftwood lying all along it above the tide line and nobody living anywhere near. The men are all looking at you.
I will carry wood for him, and I will not ask which god the fire is for.
Put in, and burn him here
Give him to the water after all
Not here, we will carry him further on

It takes until dark to gather enough wood, and he burns slowly at first and then all at once. You throw his rune sticks into the fire after him one at a time, and nobody can read what any of them said.
You give him to the water with his bag of rune sticks tied to his belt, and most of the sticks float away on their own.
You sail on, and he lies under the foredeck as before.
The Wōkerer's door

The Wōkerer's house stands on the dam with its back to the river. The two men with the rope will be in the yard, unless they are out looking for somebody, and he will be sitting at his table as he always is.
God keep you. I did not see you come up to the house, and I will not have seen you leave it either, which is all that I can do for you.
Call the one who did it out into the yard
Go in to him at his table
Not today
He comes out because somebody called him, and he brings the rope with him. He does not seem to understand what it is about until it is nearly over.
There are more than two of them in the yard today, and you have to fight your way back down to the boat. Not all of you reach it.
He looks up from his dish and begins to count something, and then he loses the count. You put both halves of your stick on his fire, and nobody in the house tries to stop you from leaving.
He does not even get up from the table, and he goes on eating while his men carry you out of the house.
You stand across the way and look at the house for a while, and then you go back down to the boat.
Before the count
The count hears pleas in the hall beside the mint. Yours comes between a quarrel over a boundary ditch and a man who has lost a pig.
So he was a Dane with no kin in this land, and he was killed by a Frisian's men over a Frisian's debt, which is your debt. All the same he was a free man, so tell me what you are asking for.
Ask a free man's price for him
Leave the hall and settle it in blood
Not today
The count sets it at the price of a free man and has it taken off your own stick. The Wōkerer's man makes his mark to agree to it, and nobody in the hall says Ravn's name.
The Wōkerer has brought six men who swear that it was only a quarrel among sailors, and you have nobody but yourself. The count tells you to come back when you have more than that.
You walk out past the man who lost his pig, and nobody tries to stop you.
You decide not to go in today.
The count's men
Two of the count's men are standing on the quay before your lines are even made fast, and it is plain that they know your boat.
You are the one who killed the lender of Dorestat at his own table. The count has set his price on you at four pounds, and until you pay it, nothing you own is yours in this land.
Pay the count his price (960 d)
Let them take what is in the hold
Tell them they have the wrong boat
They count it out on the quay, which takes them a long time. Then one of them wishes you God's keeping, as if nothing had ever happened.
They empty the hold right down to the ballast stones.
They look at your boat and then at each other, and they agree that there are a great many boats that look like this one.
They tell you that they know perfectly well which boat this is.
He told us to say sorry about the Dane... no, wait, he told us not to say sorry about the Dane.
The one who did it
It is the same two men as before, and the one with the rope is the one who killed Ravn. He does not look as if he has thought about it since.
You again! Where is the one with the sticks today? Oh, no, wait, I remember now.
Kill him
Not now
It is over before the other one has even put down the rope. The man who killed Ravn sits down on the planks just as Ravn did, and Bubo looks at his shoes.
He is slower than you are, but it does not help you, because the other one takes you by the neck from behind. When it is over, one of your own men is lying on the planks.
You let him stand there, although you know exactly where he is for as long as he stays.
God keep you! My name is Bubo, and I keep the tally stick for him, so I am here to count whatever you give us.
The Wōkerer said that the third time we come, it is the Dane. Is this the third time?
It is the third time. I counted it twice to be sure, and I am sorry for it.
Now sit down a moment, the pair of you, for I've a riddle you'll not have heard. What is it that has only one eye, and goes about the w
The one with the rope has put his knife in under Ravn's beard.
Ravn! Look at me, old friend, look at me!
Ravn opens his mouth to answer him, and no sound comes out of it.
Our Father in heaven... I am sorry, Ravn, it is the only prayer I know.
Aldger makes the sign of the cross over him. Ravn sees him do it, and he cannot tell him to stop.
Do we take the boat as well now?
No, we go home now. God keep you all.
Ravn is dead.
